t: Most Visited Sector in a Circular Track — Only the Start and End Matter
o: We walk a circular track of n sectors, visiting sectors in ascending order and wrapping back to 1 after n. The marathon is described by consecutive segments; we must return all sectors visited the most times, sorted ascending. The key observation: every full lap adds exactly one visit to *every* sector, so full laps never change which sectors are most visited. Therefore only the partial path from the starting sector `rounds[0]` up to the final sector `rounds[m]` matters. In Example 1, we go 1→2→3→4→1→2; stripping the full lap leaves 1→2, so [1,2]. In Example 3 there are no wraps: 1→2→3→4→5→6→7. Constraints are tiny (n, m ≤ 100), so even simulation works, but the O(n) insight-based solution is trivial.
k: Each complete lap visits every sector exactly once, so laps contribute uniformly and can be ignored when finding the maximum-visited sectors.
The answer is simply the sectors encountered walking forward from rounds[0] to rounds[last], wrapping around n if needed.
The result is naturally produced in ascending order by iterating i = rounds[0], rounds[0]+1, ... modulo n.

a.i: Simulate the marathon literally: for each segment between consecutive rounds entries, step sector by sector (wrapping via modulo) and count visits in an array. Then collect all sectors with the maximum count. With n, m ≤ 100 this is at most ~10,000 steps — perfectly fine.
s: Create a count array of size n+1 initialized to zero.
For each i from 0 to m-1, walk from rounds[i] to rounds[i+1], incrementing counts (wrap with modulo).
Return all sectors whose count equals the max, in ascending order.
a.t: O(m·n) — each segment can traverse up to n sectors, and m ≤ 100.
a.sp: O(n) — the visit-count array plus output.

a.n: Approach 2: O(n) Insight — Walk From Start to End
a.i: Since every full lap adds one visit to all sectors equally, it cannot affect which sectors are maximal. Strip away whole laps: the relative ranking depends only on the final partial arc from rounds[0] forward to rounds[last]. So just enumerate that arc (wrapping around), which is already in ascending order — no counting or sorting needed.
s: Starting from s, repeatedly move to the next sector (mod n, mapping 0 back to n) until reaching e, collecting each visited sector including both endpoints.
Return the collected list directly — it is already sorted ascending.
a.t: O(n) — the arc from s to e contains at most n sectors, independent of m.
a.sp: O(1) extra space besides the output list.

w: In an interview, mention the brute-force simulation first to show correctness, then derive the O(n) insight — interviewers love the observation that full laps cancel out. Pitfalls: forgetting to count the starting sector rounds[0] itself as visited; off-by-one errors when wrapping (use `cur = cur % n + 1`, not `(cur % n) + 1` confusion); assuming the answer needs sorting (the forward walk already yields ascending order). Edge cases: start equals end after many laps (answer is a single sector, e.g. Example 2), and a single segment spanning the whole track (Example 3). A likely follow-up: what if sectors were visited clockwise or the track were huge — the same insight still gives O(arc length).
